The '''Town of Haverstraw''' ({{IPA|en|ˈhæːvəɹstɹɔː|audio|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Noaius Paticus-Haverstraw.wav}}) is a [[Administrative divisions of New York#Town|town]] in [[Rockland County, New York]], United States, located north of the [[Clarkstown, New York|Town of Clarkstown]] and the [[Ramapo, New York|Town of Ramapo]]; east of [[Orange County, New York|Orange County]]; south of the [[Stony Point, New York|Town of Stony Point]]; and west of the [[Hudson River]]. The town runs from the west to the east border of the county in its northern section. The population was 39,087 at the 2020 census.<ref>U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Report, Haverstraw, Rockland County, New York QuickFacts https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/haverstrawtownrocklandcountynewyork Accessed January 8, 2023</ref>

The name comes from the Dutch word ''Haverstroo'' meaning "oats straw",<ref>{{cite book | url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_9V1IAAAAMAAJ | title=The Origin of Certain Place Names in the United States | publisher=Govt. Print. Off. | author=Gannett, Henry | year=1905 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_9V1IAAAAMAAJ/page/n151 152]}}</ref> referring to the grasslands along the river. The town contains three [[Administrative divisions of New York#Village|villages]], one of which is also known as [[Haverstraw (village), New York|Haverstraw]]. Haverstraw village is the original seat of government for the town, hosting the area's historic central downtown business district and the densest population in northern Rockland County.
[[File:ROCKLAND PRINT WORKS HISTORIC DISTRICT. HAVERSTRAW, ROCKLAND COUNTY, NY.jpg|thumb|left|Built in 1828 by the Graner brothers as a calico printing plant 30 building complex - known now as Garnerville Arts and Industrial Center]]
==History==
In 1609, the region was explored by [[Henry Hudson]]. A land purchase was made in this town in 1666 from local natives and confirmed as a patent in 1671.  The region was known as ''Haverstroo'', meaning "oat straw" in [[Dutch language|Dutch]].<ref name="Website-1">{{Cite web |title=Welcome to The Town of Haverstraw - Rockland County, NY |url=https://www.townofhaverstraw.gov/history.html |access-date=2026-10-24 |website=www.townofhaverstraw.gov}}</ref>

During the [[American Revolution]], it served (under the command of [[Col. Ann Hawkes Hay]]) as an important lookout for British activities on the Hudson. A blue-marked trail, the Long Path, may be taken {{convert|2|mi|0}} eastward from Central Highway along the crest of South Mountain to High Tor. Halfway is Little Tor, the second highest peak on South Mountain.<ref name="Website-1" />

The town of Haverstraw was formed in 1788 while still part of [[Orange County, New York]].  Haverstraw was partitioned in 1791 to form the town of [[Clarkstown, New York|Clarkstown]] and the town of [[Ramapo, New York|Ramapo]] and again in 1865 to form the town of [[Stony Point, New York|Stony Point]].<ref name="Website-1" />

In 1826 the town was the site of a short-lived effort to establish an [[List of Owenite communities in the United States|Owenite colony]] called the [[Franklin Community]].<ref name=Bestor>Arthur Bestor, ''Backwoods Utopias: The Sectarian Origins and the Owenite Phase of Communitarian Socialism in America, 1663-1829.'' [1950] Enlarged 2nd Edition. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1970; pp. 203-204.</ref> Underfinanced and wracked by internal dissent, the model Owenite community folded after a mere five months of operation.<ref name=Bestor />

In 1988, Thomas L. Watson Sr. was elected mayor of Haverstraw, making history as the first African American elected village mayor in New York State.<ref name="PatchWatsonObit2">{{cite news |last=Patch Staff |date=2019-11-05 |title=Obituary: The Honorable Thomas L. Watson Sr. |url=https://patch.com |access-date=2026-10-10 |work=Patch New City |quote=In 1988, Mr. Watson made history as the first African American elected Mayor of a Village in New York State.}}</ref><ref name="News12Watson2">{{cite news |date=2019-11-07 |title=Dozens gather to mourn first African-American mayor in New York |url=https://news12.com |access-date=2026-10-10 |work=News 12 Long Island |quote=Thomas Watson served as mayor of Haverstraw from 1989 until 1995... made history as the first African-American mayor of a village in the state of NY.}}</ref><ref name="HaverstrawRecords2">{{cite web |date=2019-10-31 |title=The Village Remembers Mayor Thomas Watson Sr. |url=https://villageofhaverstraw.gov |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=The Village of Haverstraw}}</ref> Watson assumed office in January 1989 and served until 1995.

Haverstraw has one of largest Dominican communities in the United States with Dominicans making up 32.4% of the population<ref>{{cite web |title=Data Access and Dissemination Systems (DADS) |url=http://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=DEC_10_SF1_QTP10&prodType=table |website=Factfinder.census.gov |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200212213707/http://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=DEC_10_SF1_QTP10&prodType=table |archive-date=February 12, 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

There were 11,255 households, out of which 37.3% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 54.4% were married couples living together, 15.0% had a female householder with no husband present, and 26.0% were non-families. 21.3% of all households were made up of individuals, and 7.8% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older.  The average household size was 2.94 and the average family size was 3.43.<ref name="Website-2">{{Cite web |title=U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts: Haverstraw town, Rockland County, New York |url=https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/haverstrawtownrocklandcountynewyork |access-date=2026-10-24 |website=www.census.gov |language=en}}</ref>

In the town, the population was spread out, with 26.3% under the age of 18, 8.6% from 18 to 24, 31.2% from 25 to 44, 23.6% from 45 to 64, and 10.3% who were 65 years of age or older.  The median age was 35 years. For every 100 females, there were 93.7 males.  For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 89.4 males.<ref name="Website-2" />

The median income for a household in the town was $53,850, and the median income for a family was $61,119. Males had a median income of $40,109 versus $31,979 for females. The per capita income for the town was $22,188.  About 8.1% of families and 10.6% of the population were below the poverty line, including 12.8% of those under age 18 and 13.8% of those age 65 or over.<ref name="Website-2" />

As of the 2020 census, there were 39,087 people residing in the town.<ref>[https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/haverstrawtownrocklandcountynewyork Haverstraw town, Rockland County, New York]</ref>

==Government==
Haverstraw has a council form of government.  The town supervisor is Howard T. Phillips Jr., and council members are Vincent Gamboli, John J. Gould, Hector L. Soto and Isidro "Papo" Cancel.  The town's services include a police department.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Haverstraw, New York |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Haverstraw,_New_York |access-date=2026-10-24 |website=Ballotpedia |language=en}}</ref>

==Transportation==

Major highways include the [[Palisades Interstate Parkway]], [[U.S. Route 9W]], [[U.S. Route 202]], and [[New York State Route 45|NY Route 45]]. Haverstraw is also a terminus of the [[NY Waterway]]/[[Metro-North Railroad]] [[Haverstraw–Ossining Ferry]].
[[Short Line (bus company)|Short Line]], part of [[Coach USA]], provides daily service along U.S. Route 9W heading to and from the [[Port Authority Bus Terminal]] in [[Midtown Manhattan]] and [[West Point Military Academy]] or [[Newburgh (town), New York|Newburgh]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Haverstraw-Ossining Ferry |url=https://www.mta.info/agency/metro-north-railroad/connecting-services/haverstraw-ossining |access-date=2026-10-24 |website=www.mta.info |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Coach USA {{!}} Available Schedules |url=https://web.coachusa.com/coachSS/ss.listing.asp?action=Lookup&c1=New+York&s1=NY&c2=Haverstraw&s2=NY&resultId=202221&order=&dayFilter=&scheduleChoice=&nt=1&sitePageName=%2Findex%2Easp&cbid=142911830712 |access-date=2026-10-24 |website=web.coachusa.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Transportation - Explore Rockland |url=https://explorerocklandny.com/about/transportation/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305225144/https://explorerocklandny.com/about/transportation/ |archive-date=2026-03-05 |access-date=2026-10-24 |work=Explore Rockland |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[File:New York Central Herald.png|thumb|left|110px|The [[West Shore Railroad]] provided commuter service until 1959.]]

[[New York Central]]'s [[West Shore Railroad]] began operations along the banks of the Hudson in 1883 and until 1958 operated passenger service between [[Albany, New York|Albany]] and [[Weehawken Terminal]] in [[Weehawken, New Jersey]], where passengers could transfer to ferries to [[Manhattan]].<ref name=intercity>{{cite web   | title = Intercity passenger trains serving New York via New Jersey terminals in 1942, 1956, and 1971 immediately prior to the creation of Amtrak.   | work = New York's Passenger Trains of the Past   | url = http://web.me.com/willvdv/chirailfan/stbcjcy.html | access-date = February 13, 2012 }}</ref> Service between West Haverstraw and Weehawken was discontinued in 1959. The [[right of way (transportation)|right of way]] is still used for freight and is known as the River Line. [[River Line (Conrail)|Conrail]] operated the system until its dissolution. It is now part of the [[River Subdivision (CSX Transportation)|CSX River Subdivision]] which runs between [[North Bergen Yard]] in New Jersey and [[Selkirk, New York]].

==Education==
{{expand section|date=May 2020}}
The [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York]] operates Catholic schools in Rockland County. St. Peter Parish School was in Haverstraw. In 2012, after the archdiocese announced that it could potentially be closed, the school community did a fundraising drive as the school was told it could remain open if a plan to raise $500,000 annually was produced. That year the school's per-student cost was $5,500 but it relied on archdiocese funds as it deliberately had tuition below cost, at $3,600,<ref name=Haverstrawsupporters>{{cite web|url=https://www.lohud.com/article/20121222/NEWS03/312220068/St-Peter-s-supporters-Haverstraw-use-Facebook-YouTube-bid-save-school|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130121005349/https://www.lohud.com/article/20121222/NEWS03/312220068/St-Peter-s-supporters-Haverstraw-use-Facebook-YouTube-bid-save-school|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 21, 2013|title=St. Peter's supporters in Haverstraw use Facebook, YouTube in bid to save school|newspaper=[[Lower Hudson Journal News]]|date=December 22, 2012|access-date=May 5, 2020}}</ref> so children of [[working class]] backgrounds could attend. It had an increasing enrollment at the time of closure, with 328 students in its final year.<ref name=Ottermanmoreclosing>{{cite web|author=Otterman, Sharon|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/15/education/catholic-schools-in-new-york-await-more-closing-bells.html?ref=sharonotterman|title=Catholic Schools Await More Closing Bells|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=January 15, 2013|access-date=May 5, 2020}}</ref>
